question_text: Compare the rate at which oxygen ions diffuse in alumina $\left(\mathrm{Al}_2 \mathrm{O}_3\right)$ with the rate at which aluminum ions diffuse in $\mathrm{Al}_2 \mathrm{O}_3$ at $1500^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Explain the difference. Give your answer as a tuple: (oxygen_diffusion_rate, aluminum_diffusion_rate).The units of each required answer are (cm²/s, cm²/s), respectively.
response:
## Reasoning

For self-diffusion in α-Al₂O₃ (corundum), I use the established Arrhenius data $D = D_0\exp(-Q/RT)$ with $R=1.987\;\text{cal/(mol·K)}$ and $T=1500+273=1773\;\text{K}$:

| Species | $D_0$ (cm²/s) | $Q$ (cal/mol) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| O²⁻ in Al₂O₃ | $2.0\times10^{-3}$ | $110{,}000$ | Oishi & Kingery |
| Al³⁺ in Al₂O₃ | $2.8\times10^{5}$ | $138{,}000$ | Paladino & Kingery |

$$D_{\mathrm O}=2.0\times10^{-3}\,e^{-110000/(1.987\cdot1773)}\approx 5.5\times10^{-17}\;\text{cm}^2/\text{s}$$

$$D_{\mathrm{Al}}=2.8\times10^{5}\,e^{-138000/(1.987\cdot1773)}\approx 2.7\times10^{-12}\;\text{cm}^2/\text{s}$$

So $D_{\mathrm{Al}}/D_{\mathrm O}\approx 5\times10^{4}$ — **aluminum ions diffuse roughly $50{,}000\times$ faster than oxygen ions** at 1500 °C.

**Why the difference:** The corundum structure consists of a nearly hexagonal close‑packed array of large O²⁻ anions, with the smaller Al³⁺ cations occupying two‑thirds of the octahedral interstices. Moving an O²⁻ ion requires forcing a large ion through a densely packed anion sublattice — a very high activation barrier. The much smaller Al³⁺ ions move through the more open cation sublattice (via cation vacancies) with a far lower barrier, so they are the mobile species. This is why Al³⁺ is the faster (rate‑controlling) diffuser in alumina.

$$\boxed{(5.5\times10^{-17},\;2.7\times10^{-12})}$$
